sections.heading: DEFINITION
content: According to the Digital Twin Consortium, a digital twin is a virtual representation of real-world entities and
processes, synchronized at a specified frequency and fidelity. This allows end users to monitor what is
happening inside the physical asset in real time. By providing a holistic view of real-time behavior in a real-
world environment mapped to a constantly updated virtual model, digital twins make it possible to
anticipate maintenance needs, optimize performance, and avoid costly failures.
1 Micromarkets are defined as the segments and subsegments of the digital twin market included in the scope of the report.
2 Core competencies of companies are captured in terms of their key developments and strategies adopted to sustain their positions in the market.

sections.heading: DIGITAL TWIN MARKET - GLOBAL FORECAST TO 2027
content: JUNE 2022 © MarketsandMarkets™
A digital twin accurately replicates the real-time performance of an equipment, system, person, or process.
It functions in the present, mimicking the physical thing but with complete knowledge of its past
performance as well as an exact assessment of its future potential. A digital twin's ability to test scenarios
is a vital feature. Data consumers can utilize a digital twin to test various scenarios and examine the
outcomes and implications without putting themselves in danger in the real world. Users can run "what if"
scenarios all the way up and down the supply chain and production process to see which tactics are the
most profitable. The digital twin technology enables to create a virtual replica of a physical asset,
component, product, process, or system/unit. It utilizes the data obtained from several sensors in the
systems or asset, integrates various technologies such as IoT, IIoT, AI, AR/VR, ML, and big data analytics
for analysis, and makes reasonable projections about the future process. A digital twin is used in the
design and development, simulation, and operational & maintenance phase of any product or system. It
helps in reducing the operating cost and extending the life of equipment and assets used in manufacturing

Digital twins are used for various applications such as predictive maintenance, business optimization,
performance monitoring, inventory management, product design & development, and others. Initially, end
users were mainly using digital twins for performance monitoring. However, according to present trends, it
is expected that end-user industry players will use digital twin solutions more for predictive maintenance

sections.heading: and business optimization.
content: The global digital twin market was estimated at USD 4,500 million in 2021 and is projected to reach USD
73,500 million by 2027, registering a CAGR of 60.6% from 2022 to 2027. The market has been
segmented based on application, industry, enterprise, and region. Rising emphasis on digital twin in
manufacturing industries to reduce cost and improve supply chain; and increasing demand for digital twins
from the healthcare and pharmaceuticals industries are the major drivers for the market. The growing
importance of advanced real-time data analytics and increasing adoption of smart manufacturing/industry
4.0 principles on a global scale creates future scope for the digital twin market. On the other hand, the
high investment cost involved in implementing digital twin technology is a major factor restraining the
growth of the market. In addition, the system complexities, availability of accurate mathematical models,
and unified data structure are major challenges for the market players.
Product launches, deals (mergers, acquisitions, partnerships, cooperation, alliances, collaborations,
agreements, contracts, and investments), and others (expansions) were the major growth strategies
adopted by the players in the digital twin market. These strategies enabled the players to efficiently cater
to the growing demand for digital twin from end users and expand their global footprint by offering their
products in all the major regions.
Key players in the digital twin market are General Electric (US), Microsoft (US), Siemens (Germany),
Amazon Web Services (US), ANSYS (US), Dassault Systèmes (France), PTC (US), Robert Bosch (Germany),
Oracle (US), DNV (Norway), Autodesk (US), SAP (Germany), Emerson (US), ABB (Switzerland), Honeywell
(US), IBM (US), Johnson Controls (Ireland), Schneider Electric (France), Software AG (Germany), NavVis

sections.heading: PREDICTIVE MAINTENANCE SEGMENT TO HOLD LARGEST SHARE OF DIGITAL
TWIN MARKET, BY APPLICATION, DURING FORECAST PERIOD

content: Source: Secondary Research, Interviews with Experts, and MarketsandMarkets Analysis
The predictive maintenance application is expected to account for the largest size of the digital twin market
during the forecast period. It is further expected to grow at the second-highest CAGR during the forecast
period. Every organization needs their key equipment to operate at peak efficiency and utilization to realize
their return on capital expenditures. This is the fundamental cause for the emergence of predictive
maintenance applications of digital twin. With digital twin, companies are focusing on developing a
predictive maintenance model that optimizes the maintenance cycle and strikes a balance between
corrective and preventative maintenance.

sections.heading: SMALL & MEDIUM ENTERPRISES SEGMENT TO REGISTER HIGHEST CAGR

content: Source: Secondary Research, Interviews with Experts, and MarketsandMarkets Analysis
The small & medium enterprises segment is expected to dominate the market throughout the forecast
period. Many startups are offering digital twin products/solutions that are cost-efficient to some extent
and, therefore, a perfect fit for SMEs. For instance, Pratiti Technologies (India) offers cost-efficient digital
twin solutions for the renewable energy industry. QiO Technologies (UK) offers PARCs and Digital Health
Record algorithms to businesses to measure and benchmark their asset performance, and continuously
rank the next best actions. The firm provides multi-platform compatibility as well as the ability to install on
any cloud or internet of things (IoT) platform. Interoperability with legacy information technology (IT) and
operational technology (OT)systems is a key feature of the solutions.

The digital twin market for healthcare industry is expected to grow at the highest CAGR during the forecast
period. The rapid growth of the healthcare sector is due to the increasing value of patient safety and
advancements in the patient care systems with the integration of technologies, such as internet of things
(IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and extended reality (XR). In addition, the use of digital twins is also growing
for monitoring, diagnostics, and prognostics; for example, digital twins of organs such as the heart, lung,
and brain are developed that help surgeons and doctors to test various parameters on the twin and then
implement it in the real-life situation.

automation in industries; growing adoption of technologies such as IoT and Industrial IoT (IIoT); and the
increasing need to optimize productivity and reduce operational and maintenance costs. North America is
one of the early adopters of digital twin technology. The region leads in terms of advanced automation
technology and the use of digital twin and related/complementary technologies. All these factors
contribute to the growth of the digital twin market in North America.

sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
content: This chapter focuses on the analysis of the digital twin market dynamics—drivers, restraints, opportunities,
challenges, the supply chain, ecosystem, Porter’s Five Forces analysis, technology trends, average selling
price, trade analysis, patent analysis, and tariffs and regulations. Digital twins optimize the product
performance by modifying the physical prototype and, hence, reduce the time and cost required for product
development. Digital twin technology also facilitates the linking of the physical environment with the virtual
environment of the product using technologies such as cloud computing, machine learning, and industrial
internet of things (IIoT). Digital twin technology allows for the development/creation of a digital model of a
physical system in order to examine and assess its performance precisely. Computer-aided design tools,
bill of materials, simulation models, time-series data, IoT sensors, maintenance records, and any other
data a user/manufacturer desires to bring together are used to construct digital twins.
Rising emphasis on digital twins in manufacturing industries to reduce cost and improve supply chain
operations; increasing demand for digital twins from the healthcare industry; and growing focus on
predictive maintenance are the driving factors for the growth of digital twin market. The susceptibility of
digital twin to cyberattacks due to the use of IoT and cloud platforms hinders the growth in the market.
Presently, digital twin providers have a high growth opportunity in manufacturing industries. Further, the
rising emphasis on advanced real-time data analytics, and increasing adoption of Industry 4.0 principles
create future scope for the adoption of digital twin.

Rising emphasis on digital twin in manufacturing industries to
reduce cost and improve supply chain operations
Unplanned downtime and production waste severely affect manufacturers. Hence, they are looking for a
system that can determine possible defects and failures in advance to avoid future losses. The use of
digital twin enables to reduce the excess time and cost required in manufacturing. By implementing digital
twins, engineers can optimize a product’s performance by modifying the physical prototype that changes at
every instance during the design phase. Hence, a digital prototype created with a digital twin can be used
to run simulations and can be modified at any instance at a lesser time and with minimal costs. A digital
twin has numerous applications in manufacturing, such as configuration management, asset
management, process control, performance management, and simulation modeling.
The data that is used in digital twin technology is historical data. In few instances, the digital twin operates
with real-time data. Analysts can use digital twins to better understand a supply chain's behavior, foresee
uncommon circumstances, and create an action plan to cut down costs and increase process efficiency. A
digital twin can aid firms in recognizing trends and simulating the effects of changes to various processes
in order to improve supply chain design tests, as well as monitor risk and test probabilities. Digital twin
offers a continuous, end-to-end picture of all the processes and bottlenecks associated with the supply
chain, allowing manufacturers to solve problems faster and with minimal human intervention. These twins
collect data to assist uncover potential flaws in all phases of delivery. For instance, a shipment digital twin
will rely on data collected from sensors that communicate updated data throughout shipment, which may
be evaluated to identify performance and bottlenecks during transportation and delivery journeys.

Digital twins help supply chain management to better arrange transportation and resources by exploiting
real-time data. Furthermore, the technology allows for supply chain optimization across the entire network.
River Logic, a US-based company involved in prescriptive analytics (optimization), offers supply chain digital
twin to its customer to tackle short-, medium-, and long-term decision-making challenges. Similarly, SAP
(Germany), in partnership with Siemens (Germany), co-sells digital twin focused on production and supply
chains. As firms venture into new territory, it is critical to embrace digital twins in order to meet the
market's changing demands. It will boost the potential to take businesses to new heights by improving data
flow. Furthermore, when digital twins are combined with artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML),
and digital reality services (virtual reality/mixed reality), firms have new opportunities to incorporate lower-
level workers with greater visibility and efficiency.
Increasing demand for digital twin from healthcare industry
Digital twin plays an important role in monitoring patient health, impact of medicines and therapies, and
other parameters. Amid COVID-19, few digital twin industry players created or deployed solutions to fight
the deadly coronavirus. Exactcure (France) has developed a digital twin solution to reduce the impact of
inaccurately dosed medication and help patients avoid underdose and overdoses. Through this solution,
the efficacy and interactions of medications in the body of a patient based on their personal characteristics
such as age, gender, and kidney status are monitored. With the rapid spread of the coronavirus, the
healthcare and pharmaceuticals industries resorted to digital twin technology to combat COVID-19.
According to NavVis, a Germany-based digital twin provider, the use of NavVis Digital Twin has surged by
nearly 300% post the implementation of COVID-19 physical distancing measures. With the help of digital
twin in healthcare, many environmental, health, and safety (EHS) responsibilities, as well as layout
planning and operations, can be done from home.
Healthcare industry players and digital twin providers are increasingly investing in research and
development pertaining to new daily life changes that occurred due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Industry
players are trying to develop a digital twin solution to correctly identify people who have symptoms, are
infected, or have recovered with antibodies and people who have come in contact with an infected person.
For instance, in October 2021, Dell (US) partnered with the i2b2 tranSMART Foundation (US), an open-
source open-date community for enabling collaboration for precision medicine to create privacy-preserving
digital twins to treat the long-haul symptoms of COVID-19 patients. The study aims to enhance care for the
5% of COVID-19 patients who experience chronic health problems. By using such a solution, it will be easy
for state or local governments to monitor green and red zones. Such solutions can be deployed in smart
cities effectively. In addition, digital twin technology can also be used to create a virtual twin of a hospital in
order to analyze operational strategies, capacity, staffing, and care models. This will help hospitals to
identify the areas for improvement, predict future issues, and optimize organizational strategies. Hospital
digital twins can be utilized not only to optimize resource allocation but also for risk management. With risk
management, hospitals can create a safe environment by implementing data-driven strategic decisions in
a complex and sensitive environment.
Digital twins are also used to construct personalized medicine and treatment regimens by modeling organs
and single cells, as well as an individual's genetic makeup, physiological traits, and lifestyle patterns. For
instance, in February 2020, Dassault Systèmes (France), a digital twin provider, unveiled its digital twin,
which aims to revolutionize the healthcare for the treatment of patients by enabling virtual twin
experiences of the human body. As the next step in this revolution, in January 2022, at CES 2022 (Las
Vegas), the company showcased the virtual twin of the human brain. By providing tailored diagnosis and
treatment planning, these reproductions of the human body's internal systems improve medical care and
patient treatment. Similarly, Siemens Healthineers has developed a digital twin of the heart, which mimics
the electrical and physical properties of the cells in a patient’s heart. Cardiologist Benjamin Meder ran
simulations to see if the pacemaker can keep a person with congestive heart failure alive before inserting

Growing focus of industries on predictive maintenance
Digital twin is used widely for predictive maintenance across various industries. Digital twin-based
predictive maintenance uses real-time sensor records about the health and working conditions of a
product, process, or system/unit and analyzes it against historical data about its failure modes and their
criticality. This analyzed data is then used for predictive maintenance. Along with the prediction of failures,
the technology provides various benefits that help in optimizing the complete maintenance process. Digital
twin offers the ability to calculate maintenance-related key performance indicators. In addition, digital twin
also forecasts the behavior of machines under different circumstances. Being an accurate real-time model
for a product’s, process’s, and system’s/unit’s condition and performance, a digital twin is used to run
simulations and predict how a product, process, and system/unit will "behave" under certain factors, e.g.,
runtime, exposure to severe operating conditions, temperature, etc.
Digital twins, combined with augmented and virtual reality, help companies in better involvement of
customers at the earlier stage in the maintenance process, thereby minimizing the need for expensive late-
stage changes and saving time and money. In the aerospace industry, digital twins help minimize
maintenance costs, optimize processing, and reduce downtime. General Electric (US) has built digital twins
for airplane landing gears. The sensors placed at the landing gear failure points will help in predicting the
malfunction or diagnosing the lifecycle of the landing gear. GE Aviation is also producing a digital twin for
each engine being manufactured. This gives the engine manufacturer a digital trial for each engine, which
helps GE predict the failure of parts.
Digital twin technology offers the ability to timely recognize disruptions in asset performance, forecast
potential problems, and simulate various maintenance scenarios. It helps companies eliminate machine
downtime, reduce equipment maintenance costs, improve equipment reliability, and extend lifespan. With
the introduction of IoT and digital twins, companies are focusing on developing a predictive maintenance
model that optimizes the maintenance cycle and strikes a balance between corrective and preventative
maintenance. Components are replaced only as needed in predictive maintenance. This method not only
replaces components on the verge of failure but also extends component lifetime by lowering unscheduled
maintenance and labor expenses. This helps businesses to save money and gain a competitive advantage.
Hence, in the near future, end-user industry players will opt for digital twin solutions to avoid losses
occurring due to unavailable remote facilities.

To improve the efficiency of the primary disciplines of such systems, digital twins are increasingly being
used in smart manufacturing systems. For instance, the cost associated with the overall setup of digital
twin for electrical vehicles (EVs) and automated guided vehicles (AGVs) systems is high as these vehicles
are programmed and require navigation and communication systems to interact with other material
handling equipment. The average payback period for AGVs usually ranges from three to five years.
Therefore, it is difficult for many companies to invest in digital twin technology for AGVs due to high capital
spending and a long payback period.
Susceptibility of digital twin to cyberattacks
The implementation of digital technologies, such as the cloud, big data, IoT, and artificial intelligence, is
increasing in various facets of businesses. Digital twin involves the integration of various IoT sensors and
other digital technologies for virtualizing the physical twin. With growing connectivity arises the risk of
security, compliance, data protection, and regulations. Increasing occurrences of viruses and cyber-attacks
have raised concerns regarding data security. Important information can be stolen by malicious viruses in
computer systems, resulting in a major loss to the companies. Failure of IoT infrastructure providers and
cloud platform providers in implementing proper security measures might lead to disruptions in the flow of
information. The industries that have implemented digital twins with such platforms are prone to malware
attacks that are targeted at industrial systems due to the increasing dependence on web-based data
interchange and off-the-shelf IT solutions.
A large volume of data is more prone to the risk of security. Digital twins gather sensitive, business-critical
information from many aspects of the business into one place. Business planning needs to include data
security, data integrity, privacy, and compliance considerations. Therefore, it is essential to ensure that
good security practices are already in place while deploying digital twins, be it for a product, process, or a
complete system/unit. With the rise in cyberattacks on critical infrastructure over the past decade,
cybersecurity has become a major concern among users and vendors of industrial automation. Thus, the
increasing threat pertaining to data security is expected to be a major restraint for the growth of the digital

these issues. As the frequency of cybersecurity breaches has increased over the past years, organizations
have increased their IT security investments to protect their systems against advanced threats, zero-day
malware, and other targeted threats. However, there is a lack of framework and governance due to the
high costs of innovation pertaining to the development of advanced cybersecurity solutions. Several
organizations consider this a financial constraint, limiting the growth of the smart manufacturing market.
Thus, the deployment and maintenance of a digital twin is an expensive proposition. The lack of budget

Rising emphasis on advanced real -time data analytics
A digital twin can be used to create twins of components, assemblies, people, or an entire manufacturing
plant and can be combined in multiple ways to create a solution with numerous sources of data and
information. The foundation of digital twin technology is data and analytics. The key element of digital twin
includes the ability to monitor a real-world object and model a real-world object. Further, it is possible to
inquire for or get alerts about particular events or changes when an item may be monitored in the real
world. Whereas the ability to model a real-world object is associated with data such as identity, time,
context, and events and, thus, corresponds to a unique physical thing. All of these elements of digital twin
represent real-time data analysis that drives the operation of digital twin in any organization.
Digital twins and analytics, once established, allow for more precise diagnostic, predictive, and optimized
operations. Businesses have begun to grasp the potential of digital twins after seeing the benefits of AI and
data analytics. Currently, multiple AI and machine learning models are built to handle specific challenges,
but with a digital twin, enterprises can have access to broader business insights across the entire
organization. And due to this, digital twins are becoming a source of truth for facility insights as they take
their place in smart workplaces, at the heart of the IoT, and other network systems. Digital twin analytics is
a new standard for decision-making on how to coordinate and operate the workplace because of their
ability to contextualize data within a physical model.

Another reason for the potential growth of the digital twin market is the fact digital twins offer a sharper
vision to organizations. Predictive analytics alone may envision a simpler model that tests a set of
limited variables. However, a digital twin can be considered a more exact and complex form of a predictive
model. Digital twins use dynamic, real-time data streams instead of stored data. Furthermore, a digital twin
can take many aspects into consideration and generate a picture of the entire situation rather than simply
focusing on a small number of outcomes in a certain area.  For instance, logistic company United Parcel
Service (US) developed harmonized enterprise analytical tool (HEAT), a digital twin that operates in real-
time and predicts the resourcing needs at its facilities. Using the combination of digital twin and powerful
real-time analytics technologies, UPS manages its extremely complex logistics network by predicting and
advising actions in real time. With the help of digital twin and real-time analytics, UPS is delivering COVID-
19 vaccines to over 100 countries with 99.99% reliability.
Increasing adoption of Industry 4.0 principles
The trends of Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) and Industry 4.0/smart manufacturing are ramping up,
especially with the rising demand for digitalization. According to MarketsandMarkets, the smart
manufacturing market was estimated at USD 88.7 billion in 2021 and is expected to reach USD 228.2
billion by 2027, at a CAGR of 18.5% from 2022 to 2027. It is expected that between 2019 and 2025, the
number of global IoT connections will grow to be more than double, nearly 25 billion, while global IoT
revenue will triple to cross the USD 1.1 trillion mark (GSMA data). IoT will create enormous opportunities
for digital twin providers and their customers in the coming years.
IIoT brings together the machines, advanced analytics, and people involved in the working of a particular
process or product. This builds up a network of a multitude of industrial devices connected by
communication technologies that help to develop systems that can monitor, collect, exchange, analyze,
and deliver valuable insights for better decision-making capabilities. With the technology having the ability
to cover the entire life cycle of a physical system, process, or product, it provides businesses with a
powerful analytical tool that helps to thoroughly assess key performance indicators and provide insights as
to where enhancements/upgrades can be made. In the long run, the lessons and suggestions taken from
digital twins are expected to create immense opportunities for innovation and growth.
In addition, monitoring the field performance of the manufactured products via a digital twin along with IIoT
provides a window with an ongoing view, comparing actual usage with the anticipated usage of
manufactured products as reflected in the design parameters of the product. This process provides
valuable real-time feedback for improving the design process. The technology also increases the efficiency
of product development as the manufacturing and testing of prototypes in a physical environment
consumes not only time but also requires high investments. The virtual simulation models of the products
or processes or units make it easier for experts from various fields to participate in the product
development process. For example, software developers, mechanical engineers, and user interface
designers can all simultaneously work on the same digital twin. The deployment of IIoT and digital twins
optimizes the efficiency by predicting failures in production and helping engineering teams to fix them
before they affect manufacturing targets. Enhancements can be made and simulated by adjusting the
parameters of the production line in the digital twin itself, without causing any harm to the actual
production. Later, only the successful simulations/enhancements can then be applied to the real-life
system. For example, by using a digital twin of turbines for a wind farm, engineers can study how turbines
interact with different landscapes and wind sources, then mix and match different turbines to optimize the
configuration for each pad on a farm.

Development of human-centered digital twins
Digital twins based on human-in-the-loop (HITL) allow artificial intelligence to leverage both human and
machine intelligence to create machine learning models. This methodology allows human, product, and
system data to be linked to computational toolkits, allowing for ergonomic decision-making to be
incorporated into digital twin-driven design. When building a model, it is important to think about human
factors such as taking breaks between work sessions, taking fatigue into account, considering the working
hours, and so on. The human-centric digital twin design allows for realistic output optimization rather than
focusing solely on boosting production and efficiency without taking into account human variables. For
instance, in 2022, Kalam Innovation Hub created a human-centric digital twin for its clients, which includes
break and leisure time for the employees in the model. This aided the client in optimizing output while
keeping employees' basic needs in mind and making the workplace more human-friendly.
This type of human-centered paradigm for digital twin also allows for employee safety and medical fitness
at work. It won't just be a case of re-establishing operating systems to meet new requirements; in the
present scenario as well as in future, the safety of each individual employee in terms of social distancing
will be a far more essential factor. Siemens developed a novel approach to address the issues that
businesses are facing as a result of the COVID-19 epidemic. Companies can use Siemens’s Simatic RTLS
Real-time Locating System to measure, monitor, and maintain social distance among employees.
Companies can use the solution to control how personnel interact with one another, with the production
line, and with the plant setup in a quick and efficient manner. The integrated digital twin assists the
organization in simulating employee safety, testing, and optimizing workspace setup, validating safety
measures, and designing future-proof manufacturing lines. Hence, such human-centric digital twins act as
a lucrative opportunity for companies to deploy digital twin not just for optimizing their setup and output
but also for the safety and wellness of their employees as well.

Complexities associated with data collection and mathematical

sections.heading: models
content: Despite the obvious benefits, a major portion of organizations are yet to implement a digital twin model for
asset management and business and operation optimization. A digital twin should be able to model simple
as well as complex objects and their relationships by accurately capturing their physical properties and
simulating behaviors. For instance, the development of an electrical digital twin requires multiple inputs
from operators such as facility managers, design engineers, electrical engineers, equipment vendors, and
other parties, which adds complexity to the deployment. Obtaining the asset data from the supplier may
pose a challenge, as it requires close collaboration with multiple tiers of the supply chain. Moreover,
establishing the required level of communication in a supply chain to retrieve asset data may be
challenging to maintain. Another challenge comes from the complexity of the physical item that is to be
replicated. For instance, processes such as customer relationship management, prospect marketing, or
service delivery funnels are significantly easier to duplicate, as they involve a flow of scenarios, ideas, and
software inputs instead of moving parts that must be recorded.
In addition, detailed blueprints of historical systems, equipment failures, and other mathematical systems
are required to create a digital twin. For instance, a digital twin should be fed with data about equipment
failure modes to predict failures. Any change in equipment or asset configuration or operational state
would require remodeling of the digital twin, which increases the complexity of maintaining the digital
replica. Any modification made to the physical system would require similar changes to its digital model
and algorithms. The risk of errors may escalate with the increasing levels of complexity, as the simulation
of certain scenarios, such as the addition of new parts at the machine level or operational level changes,
may not be precise.
The main problem is obtaining data in the correct format. Classic mathematical techniques such as
Bayesian estimation or Bayesian statistics are required to construct the digital model. One of the most
significant challenges is that the majority of the world is inexperienced with Bayesian statistics.
Furthermore, the lack of unified data from the organizations worldwide is a key challenge. In a company,
data is stored in a variety of silos. The data (historical or current) required to develop a digital twin model is
accessible from clients in a variety of formats. For example, some data in a supply chain is in pdf format,
while others are in engineering models or CAD models. As a result, organizing that type of data from
various sources is a difficulty for digital twin developers.
Adopting digital twins entails considerable investments, collaboration, and sustained commitment from the
operator. Operators need to establish the required technology infrastructure such as robust IoT

sections.heading: AVERAGE SELLING PRICE TREND
content: The pricing of digital twins is different as compared to standard products or services. A digital twin is a
combination of physical assets, components, various technologies, software, and others. The cost of
building a digital twin includes digital twin software, IoT, integrated software, and training and education. In
an industry, there is no standard way to calculate the pricing of the digital twin. As a result, industry players
have different ways to charge their digital twin solutions. The cost involved to implement everything from
hardware to software is highly customizable and completely depends upon the end use case. Few industry
players adopt the node pricing strategy, whereas some charge on a monthly basis.
Node pricing does not involve upfront cost or termination fees. End users are charged on the basis of per
node and message. Node indicates a single component in the overall system or solution. For instance, the
Azure digital twin solution offered by Microsoft (US) uses the node pricing strategy. Azure digital twin is a
consumption-based service, which is based on per node (each object connected to the graph) and per
message (API calls to the Azure Digital Twins APIs, incoming messages sent to device and sensor nodes in
Azure digital twins or messages sent from Azure digital twins to other systems) pricing system. For
example, in the ecosystem of housing areas, all the nodes, such as sensors, devices, are as per Microsoft’s
Azure. Each communication sent to any of the nodes is considered as a message and is chargeable. Few
industry players are charging on a monthly basis. Based on the application and product/process/system,
the monthly charges are calculated.

content: The idea of digital twin technology revolves around the utilization of data. The major focus is on real-time
data monitoring and performing the control actions accordingly. However, it also utilizes the past or
historical data for analyzing and taking/giving predictive decisions based on previous patterns and
scenarios. For some companies/manufacturers, the implementation of a digital twin may mean investing
in the expansion of their data foundation to include things such as IoT-based sensors, a revamped IT
infrastructure, and digital solutions that allow better data management and storage or even completely
building a newer infrastructure for the digital twin of the products/processes/systems. For instance, a data
integration platform that engages an organization’s entire digital ecosystem can serve as a single critical
environment, which allows digital twin-centric data to reside, converge, and be managed.
The digital twin is based on massive, cumulative, real-time, and real-world data measurements across an
array of dimensions. These measurements can create an evolving profile of the object or process in the
digital world and provide important insights on system performance, which will help to take actions in the
physical world, such as a change in product design or manufacturing process.
Digital twin represents the convergence of the physical and the virtual world where every industrial product,
process, and/or system will get a dynamic digital representation. Throughout the product development life
cycle, right from the design phase to the deployment phase, organizations can have a complete digital

sections.heading: IOT AND IIOT
content: The Internet of Things (IoT) is an environment where complex systems are networked together in such a
way that the sensor data is transmitted over the Internet for remote monitoring and performance analysis.
Digital twin uses an IoT platform for the virtual representation of a physical asset, product, process,
machine, vehicle, device, or system. It digitally represents the data, processes, state of operation, and
lifecycle of the asset. Data is fetched from the IoT sensor mesh and further processed using various
technologies according to the desired results. Implementing IoT with digital twin offers numerous benefits
or characteristics such as better visibility, accurate prediction, what-if analysis, documentation and
communication, and integration of disparate systems.
Digital twins created in the IoT space are increasingly used for digitalizing the physical world. For instance,
GE (US) has invested in the Industrial IoT (IIoT) to increase focus on digital twins, creating virtual versions
of billions of physical assets that make a global industrial infrastructure. Digital twins are key to exploring
the impact of these insights and realizing full cost-saving benefits. Due to the increasing usage of IoT

sensors, a digital twin receives continuous, real-time data/information from the twin’s real-world object or
asset. Such one-to-one correspondence makes it possible to test future scenarios, including potential
performance enhancements, and proactively anticipate maintenance faults. Few other players such as
Microsoft (US), Amazon Web Service (US), Robert Bosch (Germany), and Siemens (Germany) are involved in
rapid development of IoT for digital twin.
By linking IIoT to digital twins, businesses can begin to collect data about the operation of the physical
system to which it is linked. Further, by gathering environmental data (such as location and configuration)
and general information (such as service records, financial models, and so on) IIoT are more than capable
to enrich the digital twin. IoT and IIoT sensors collect the data from physical sources and send them over to
the server or cloud for further analysis. The Industry 4.0 revolution has had a high impact on the
manufacturing industries; it is considerably changing the traditional process of designing industrial
machines. The digital twin is one of the aspects of the Industry 4.0 strategy that supports the easy
implementation of technologies in the manufacturing and process industries and enables the companies
to enhance the efficiency of their processes. A digital twin is at the core of this industrial revolution bringing
in unlimited possibilities. It changes the traditional approach of “the first build and then tweak” in the
industrial world and brings in a more virtual system-based design process that adds much more efficient
role out of any equipment or system by understanding its unique features, performance, and potential
issues, if any. Moreover, with a digital twin, an operator can be trained on a virtual machine without the
help of a dedicated trainer or simulator.

sections.heading: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) AND MACHINE LEARNING (ML)
content: Machine learning and artificial intelligence are the two approaches that have been leveraging the concept
of big data and the IoT. A digital twin is created with the help of data collected from various sensors
attached to the assets/products, processes, and/or systems regarding their attributes/desired
parameters. This data is collected on a cloud platform and organized into a model called “twin,” which
creates the digital model that has the capability to analyze the physical asset and replicate the machine
performance in real time.
Machine learning is an application of artificial intelligence (AI) that provides systems with the ability to
automatically learn and improve from experience without being explicitly programmed. In addition to
rapidly analyzing disparate pieces of data, machine learning can automate and improve complex analytical
tasks. It can evaluate data in real time, adjust behavior with minimal need for supervision, and increase
outcome efficiency and accuracy. These features of AI & ML are used for implementing digital twin and
gaining accurate/precise analysis, monitoring, predictive measure, and for real-time detection and control
of defects or faults.
Additionally, machine learning is used to identify anomalies, signatures, and trends in machine
performance and develop an understanding of patterns of behavior. It can be applied to help identify the
performance of any asset/product, process, or system and use this as the best practice for others in the
near future. For instance, digital twins can be implemented by the energy & utilities industry with the help
of AI and ML technologies as AI has the potential to manage the accelerating influx of renewables,
distributed energy resources. On the other hand, ML can be learned based on the actual real-world
behavior of the power plant equipment under all conditions, including seasonal variations, different
operating campaigns, start-up/shutdown, and changing duty cycles. It can also consider the deteriorating
process and mechanical performance. ML mines the process and asset data for early warning.

sections.heading: EXTENDED REALITY: AUGMENTED REALITY, VIRTUAL REALITY, AND
MIXED REALITY
content: Augmented reality (AR) is a technology that integrates digital information with the user's environment in
real time, uses the existing environment, and creates a virtual model of it. To develop and design the digital
twin of a physical asset or process, an augmented reality interface interacts simultaneously with the
physical asset in real time. Any appropriate augmented reality interface such as a headset, smart glasses,
and tablets or smartphones, could be used for creating a digital twin model. Through these interfaces,
users can gain access to design data, service data, and simulation analysis as well as to the results
obtained from big data analytics. Further, the data can be projected directly on the augmented reality-
based model of an asset or a system. In the near future, augmented reality will have the potential to create
on-site interaction of digital twin, along with a virtual product linked to its product knowledge base.
Augmented reality, virtual reality (VR), extended reality (XR), and mixed reality (or hybrid – including both AR
& VR) basically add value to the user interface of that particular digital twin. Extended reality (XR) refers to
all real-and-virtual mixed settings and human-machine interactions enabled by computer technology and
wearables. VR, AR, and MR are all examples of extended reality.
By using the data provided by sensors for physical assets, a 3D model is created and projected in a virtual
environment. The virtual reality supports the digital twin technology in creating a virtual representation of
the process and asset. Data deficiencies, such as anomalies or faults, can be traced immediately by
analyzing this asset information. This allows the user to interact and control/monitor the twin in a better

sections.heading: 5G
content: 5G technology would be a key enabler for the Internet of Things (IoT) by providing a platform to connect a
large number of sensors, devices, and actuators with strict energy and transmission constraints. The digital
twin is an integration of various technologies, such as IoT, IIoT, machine learning, and cloud/edge
computing, according to the desired outcome or requirement. 5G plays a vital role in all these technologies;
data transfer plays a major and important role in its performance. In addition, the 5G infrastructure
enabled the support for mission-critical services that require high reliability, global coverage, and/or low

sections.heading: latency features.
content: The continuous increase in the number of IoT-connected devices is expected to be an opportunity for 5G
technology. To provide high bandwidth to several use cases, the 5G technology is expected to operate at
higher frequency bands, leading to the adoption of small cell network concept. However, the multi-cell
interference is one of the challenges in the ultra-dense small-cell network, which the 5G infrastructure is
still dealing with. For developing a responsive, near real-time digital twin necessitates low latency and
enormous data volumes, both of which 5G ultra-wideband and multi-access edge computing (MEC) can
provide. Verizon (US) is one such telecom operator that is providing 5G connectivity for the digital twin.
Verizon 5G solutions enable consumers to receive rich insights from a digital twin powered by 5G. Verizon's
5G ultra-wideband network is designed to enable transformational business opportunities. The 5G digital

sections.heading: CLOUD COMPUTING AND EDGE COMPUTING
content: The growing tessellation of data-generating sensors and devices, the ability to process data and create
meaningful information quickly is becoming increasingly important. Hence it becomes crucial to handle and
manage the enormous amount of data that is to be processed and analyzed. Here, cloud computing plays
a vital role. It leverages the power of the Internet to eliminate the need for purchasing, installing, and
maintaining independent data centers and networks. The utilization of cloud with IIoT infrastructure offers
manufacturers several benefits, such as data monitoring, increasing profit margin, reducing overheads,
and enhancing the scalability for discrete manufacturing. Companies optimize maintenance, predict
important maintenance events, and stimulate innovation through actual performance feedback by
constructing a virtual model of a physical product and mimicking its real-time operation. Because
simulation necessitates vast amounts of computer resources and data outputs, cloud computing has long
been the technology environment of choice for supporting digital twins due to its scalability and low cost.
Cloud computing also helps in better decision-making with real-time asset tracking.
Edge computing, on the other hand extends the centralized cloud paradigm by bringing compute capacity
closer to the data source via regionalized or local edge nodes. As a result, the users enjoy multiple benefits
with their digital twin such as better speed, privacy & regulations, and uptime in the local area. Edge
computing has emerged as a viable option in the present scenarios. Edge computing takes advantage of
local resources close to the actual product's location, resulting in lower latency and increased
responsiveness, agility, and privacy. According to ANSYS (US), a leading digital twin provider, these benefits
of edge computing can act as driver for the firms interested in developing digital twins and begin capturing
useful data about their operations. Microsoft (US), Amazon Web Services (US), ANSYS (US), and IBM (US)
are few companies that offer cloud computing and edge computing for digital twin solutions.

sections.heading: BLOCKCHAIN
content: Blockchain is a distributed ledger system that records all transactions in a digital ledger, which is publicly
available and evenly distributed to all the participants in the network. In the blockchain, a block consists of
a hash of the previous block, a time-stamp, usually both included in the header, and a payload, which is
limited in size. This payload can carry information, such as texts, data, or references to other data sources.
The blockchain is a decentralized & peer-to-peer nodes network, where each node individually holds the
entire transaction history, i.e., the entire blockchain. Hence, there is a dispersed and redundant database
for which no intermediary or central authority is required to guarantee the authenticity of transactions. A
consensus-based validation of transactions secures the uniqueness of a transaction.

Blockchain plays an important role in digital twin technology when the authenticity and identity of the
product, process, or system are of utmost importance. Creating a digital twin on the blockchain means that
all information regarding a product, process, and/or system can be saved immutably. Platform security of
the digital twin platform and data is crucial. The blockchain technology offers security from hackers due to
its encryption features and provides data history transparency. Blockchain technology allows IoT
ecosystems to move away from the traditional intermediary-based networking paradigm, in which devices
rely on a centralized cloud server to identify and authenticate individual devices. It allows the
establishment of secure networks in which IoT devices exchange commercial information in order to
complete each transaction. Further, blockchain technology supports the establishment of a scalable
network capable of supporting billions of devices without the need for extra resources. Digital twins will
benefit from these features, as it can transmit data securely. Both SMEs and large companies have started
utilizing blockchain technology to store physical objects and connecting digital twin technology for their
products, processes, and systems.
Digital twins on a blockchain will also help in brand protection and counterfeit items. Creating a digital twin
of a product on the blockchain will help to view its saved transaction records and information regarding the
place of manufacturing and previous owners. In addition, companies that will combine blockchain with
virtual simulations will be able to track their product globally with extreme accuracy. For instance, in August
2020, Honeywell (US) deployed blockchain technology for label printers to enhance the security of the
supply chains. The iTRACE 2DMI solution can be printed, authenticated, and registered to the blockchain
directly on the Honeywell PX940v Industrial Printer, allowing secure product authentication and track &
trace along the supply chain. This integration connects the physical printed item to the digital ledger,

sections.heading: THREAT OF NEW ENTRANTS
content: The threat of new entrants in the digital twin market is low. Well-established software/solution providers
such as Microsoft (US), AWS (US), Siemens (Germany), General Electric (US), ANSYS (US), and Dassault
Systèmes (France) bring innovation and continuous R&D in the digital twin market to reduce the operating
and manufacturing costs for their clients and increase the optimization and reliability. The industry requires
huge capital investment, along with patented technologies and critical expertise in mathematical
modelling, and, hence, the threat of new entrants is low. Also, the need for precise and complex algorithms
(artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning), mathematical models, and supporting
technologies poses high barriers, making it extremely difficult for new entrants to enter and sustain in the
market. Substantial investment must be made in the R&D of systems and solutions, as well as data
analytics and related technologies, to adhere to the standards regularly. This reduces the window for
profits for new firms and can reduce the threat of new entrants in the industry.

sections.heading: THREAT OF SUBSTITUTES
content: The threat of substitutes is relatively low in the digital twin market. The digital twin technology itself is a
substitute to old and traditional methods of performance monitoring and maintenance. More substitutes in
the industry result in reduced cost and profitability. Digital twins enhance operational decisions with real-
time insights derived from asset and business operations data. Furthermore, digital twin offers more
advanced features with real-time insights using Industry 4.0 technologies such as IIoT, AI, ML, and big data
analytics and is a complete packaged solution as compared to the traditional systems. The threat of
substitutes remains high if the substitutes provide more price-to-performance tradeoff and the buyer’s
switching cost is low. There are fewer traditional substitute products and fewer substitute providers in this
industry, so the threat of substitutes and the chances of customers switching to substitute competitors are
low. Customers switch to substitutes when:

sections.heading: BARGAINING POWER OF BUYERS
content: The bargaining power of buyers refers to the pressure that end users of digital twins can exert on the
developers and providers of digital twin products/solutions. The bargaining power of buyers is moderate in
the digital twin market. The more substitutes or competitors in the market, the more is the bargaining
power of the buyer. When the buyers are in large proportion and the product is slightly differentiated, the
bargaining power of the buyer becomes significant because the cost of switching can be high due to
customization requirements. Customers always get to choose from whom they want the services. In the
case of the digital twin market, the dynamics of aerospace, automotive & transportation, energy & utilities,
infrastructure, and other end-user industries are changing rapidly, which is fuels the demand for digital
twin solutions. However, there are several providers of digital twin products/solutions in the market and
offer high level of customization at variable price in the market to stay competitive. The buyers have
several options to choose from a large number of providers who offer similar digital twins at a different
price range. The buyers of digital twin solutions in emerging countries are price-sensitive; however, the
high-cost investment reduces their bargaining power. On the other hand, there are several digital twin
startups that offers digital twin at reasonable prices to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) who are
more price-sensitive as compared to large enterprises. Hence, due to the availability of more providers, the

sections.heading: BARGAINING POWER OF SUPPLIERS
content: The bargaining power of suppliers refers to the pressure that suppliers of digital twin products/solutions
can exert on end users such as utilities & grid infrastructure operators, automotive manufacturers,
pharmaceutical companies, aircraft manufacturers, smart infrastructure developers, and retailers. It also
refers to the capability of suppliers/solution providers to dictate the supply/pricing trends leveraging the
unique proposition of their digital twin solutions. The switching cost for buyers in the electrical digital twin
market is moderate. There are several global vendors offering digital twin solutions, which reduces the
bargaining power of the digital twin providers. But at the same time, digital twins are fully customized and
there is a considerable switching cost associated. These factors increase the bargaining power of digital
twin providers. Hence, the bargaining power of suppliers is moderate in the digital twin market.

sections.heading: INTEGRATING DIGITAL TWIN WITH AI-BASED PREDICTIVE MAINTENANCE INTO
Customer
content: Bell Flight, a US-based aerospace manufacturer, headquartered in Fort Worth, Texas

sections.heading: Challenge
content: Even though a piece of military gear appears to be combat ready, it may contain parts or
components that are about to fail, posing a risk that is hidden in plain sight. The company
needed a setup to detect—and even predict—risks before they have an impact on
performance and battle preparedness.

sections.heading: Solution Offered
content: IBM (US) used deep-learning AI algorithms and IoT technology like digital twin to forecast
which vehicles needed preventative maintenance. The algorithm was then able to tie
each failure prediction back to a root cause, down to the part or component level, by
feeding a variety of technical documents into that pool of data. As a result, detailed
recommendations for army aircraft maintainers may be generated automatically. The
study demonstrated how forecasting the failure of a very low-cost element can save well
over USD 12 million by avoiding the need to replace an entire system—such as an engine.
By integrating predictive insights into their ERP systems, Bell Flight can greatly improve
the way component inventories are managed. For example, in case of component flaws,
early detection is crucial. With digital twin, Bell Flight was able detect the flaws and avoid
the overestimation of the number of available parts, which could jeopardize
manufacturing and delivery schedules.

sections.heading: Result
content: The army can better manage its spare parts inventory and integrate those insights into
stronger budgeting and maintenance management procedures in the future with greater
transparency into underlying part failure trends.

advances in wind turbine development. The technology allowed Doosan to maintain its
competitive advantage and boost energy efficiency by merging data from different

sections.heading: TEMPLE UNIVERSITY USED SMART BUILDING DIGITAL TWIN FOR OPTIMIZING OPERATIONS
Customer
content: Temple University, Broad Street, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, US

sections.heading: Challenge
content: Temple University sought to create a framework for rolling out an integrated financial
management system (IFMS) over the entire campus. In addition, Temple university
needed to create a smart-building plan that would lay the groundwork for streamlining
operations across the university's 214 buildings, lowering costs, and improving services
for its schools, businesses, employees, and students.

sections.heading: Solution Offered
content: In the first phase of the project, e-Magic established a reference architecture and
implemented a working IFMS solution in five campus buildings using TwinWorX, which is
built on Azure native services. The buildings' automation, lighting, and utility metering
were connected at the edge and incorporated into the Azure cloud using Azure IoT Hub.
Temple may now oversee building operations from a single pane of glass display by
leveraging assets that were modelled using Azure Digital Twins. The university can also
draw insights from fault detection and diagnosis algorithms, Azure Time-Series Insights
analytics, and utility reporting. Temple wanted an integrated controls strategy that was
future-proof, vendor-neutral, and aligned with the IT agenda of the institution. Temple
University adopted digital twin technologies with its partner e-Magic, which leapfrogged
old solutions from embedded vendors who supplied restricted offerings at growing
costs. As a result of this, Temple University saves money on IT costs, and it will save even
more money once the platform allows for open-bid selection of building systems.

sections.heading: Result
content: Temple University is able to develop a scalable digital twins ecosystem using Azure IoT
and Azure Digital Twins, allowing the university to decrease costs and enhance operations
across the campus today and in the future as the campus grows.

content: This section represents the MFN tariffs for products with the HS code 851769 (including IoT & IIoT), which
are an integral part of the digital twin ecosystem. The most favored nation (MFN) tariff is implemented in a
country with the most favored nation status. The MFN tariff is the lowest possible tariff that a country can
impose on the products imported from another country. For example, if a country’s lowest tariff is 2% of the
value of a good, it is its MFN tariff, and the respective country charges this percentage on an import from
another country with the MFN status. Members of the World Trade Organization must extend the MFN
status to other countries that are not yet a part of the MFN list. In the US, the MFN status is formally called
permanent normal trade relations. The table below represents the data for MFN tariffs levied on products
with HS code 851769 (including IoT & IIoT).

sections.heading: DIGITAL TWIN MARKET, BY USAGE TYPE
INTRODUCTION
content: A digital twin is a virtual replica of a physical product or process that is used to better understand and
anticipate the performance characteristics of the actual process taking place in the real-world to provide
real-time feedback and insight into decision-making processes. Digital twins can demonstrate the influence
of design changes, environmental conditions, and a plethora of other variables by combining simulation,
data analysis, and machine learning skills. Depending on the extent of product magnification, many types
of digital twins exist. The types of digital twins depend upon the field of application. Different digital twins
frequently coexist within a system or process. The digital twin market, by usage type, has been segmented
into three categories: component, product, process, and system. Each type is used for various purposes,
such as designing, simulation, performance analysis, controlling, and real-time performance monitoring of
any of the abovementioned types throughout the lifecycle.
Several companies are using digital twins to detect and isolate faults, perform diagnostics and
troubleshooting, determine the ideal maintenance schedule, optimize asset operation, and generate
insights to improve the designing and performance of the next generation of the products, processes, and
systems. Digital twin has been adopted for various products, processes, and systems in different verticals,
such as aerospace, automotive & transportation, healthcare, infrastructure, oil & gas, energy & utilities,
agriculture, retail, telecommunications, and others (semiconductors, water & wastewater, chemicals, and

sections.heading: DIGITAL TWIN MARKET, BY USAGE TYPE

content: Source: Secondary Research, Expert Interviews, Company Websites, and MarketsandMarkets Analysis
The growth of the digital twin market can be attributed to the increasing use of digital twin for systems in
various industries. For example, in the aerospace sector, National Aeronautics and Space Administration
(NASA) uses digital twins to monitor its space stations and spacecraft to ensure better safety. In the
automotive & transportation sector, a start-up, SWIM AI, uses digital twins for the traffic management
system in California. Likewise, Tesla uses digital twins in the manufacturing of its cars. COVID-19 has
affected every aspect of the business for several industries such as automotive & transportation,
aerospace, oil & gas, and infrastructure, and the impact is visible on the usage type market for digital twin.
The market growth was stagnated due to the pandemic; however, COVID-19 also increased the level of
awareness about digital twin among industrial end users and the market started recovering in 2021. New
installations of products/processes/systems will continue to grow over the next four to five years. It is
expected that end users will extensively implement system/process digital twins to minimize future losses.

sections.heading: COMPONENT DIGITAL TWIN
content: The digital twin of a component/part digitally replicates the complete component based on various
parameters. The example of a component digital twin can be a bearing on a rotating piece of a motor,
rotor, engine, the heart or lung, wind turbine rotor, and control valve. Component/part twins are the
simplest example of a functioning component in a digital twin. Component twins are similar to identical
twins; however, they are for components that are slightly less important.
A component twin is linked to a larger system. For example, the bearing of an energy-producing facility.
During operation, this bearing can have a digital twin that explains its state, such as estimated mean time
between failures (MTBF) or mean time to failure (MTTF). This information can be generated (predicted or
modeled) from current data (such as vibration sensor data or sound), as well as data collected during the
design or construction process (such as what gear tooth shape was designed or what molding cutter has
been used for building it).

sections.heading: PRODUCT DIGITAL TWIN
content: The digital twin of a product digitally replicates the complete product based on various parameters. The
product twin is typically a sub-component that has a significant impact on the performance to whichever
process or system it belongs. Product/asset twins provide visibility at the equipment level. When two or
more components work together, they form an asset, and it is also referred as a resource. Product/asset
twins allow to investigate how those components interact, generating a large amount of performance data
that can be analyzed and transformed into meaningful insights.
A product twin is essentially a collection of part twins with their interactions reflected. From the standpoint
of a software product, the product twin is usually the same; hence, part twins are accessed by drilling down
from a product twin. The example of a product digital twin can be the generator of an energy production
plant. The digital twin of this generator includes many bearings component twins, among other things.
The product twin is typically a sub-component that has a significant impact on the performance to
whichever process or system it belongs. Product digital twins are mainly used for predictive maintenance or
monitoring. It provides a virtual-physical connection that lets designers, operators, and others dealing with
the product to analyze how it will perform under various conditions and make adjustments in the virtual
world to ensure that the next physical product will perform exactly as planned in the field. Product digital
twins help one to navigate any level of complexity to make the best possible decisions and necessary
control measures. All of this eliminates the need for multiple prototypes, reduces total development time,
improves the quality of the final manufactured product, and enables faster iterations in response to

sections.heading: PROCESS DIGITAL TWIN
content: Process digital twin can be a set of activities or operations, such as a manufacturing process, a surgical
process, farming process, and chemical process. A process digital twin can be informed by a set of product
twins but focuses more on the process itself rather than the equipment.
A process digital twin can help validate how well any process will work on the field before anything actually
goes into production or working conditions. These types of digital twins are mainly used for inventory
management and predictive maintenance. By simulating the process using a digital twin and analyzing why
things are happening using the digital thread, companies can create a production methodology that is
efficient for a variety of conditions and according to the desired requirements and outcomes. A digital twin
of a manufacturing process can assist assess how effectively it will perform on the shop floor before
anything goes into production. Companies can develop a manufacturing approach that stays efficient
under a variety of scenarios by recreating the process using a digital twin.

sections.heading: DIGITAL TWIN MARKET - GLOBAL FORECAST TO 2027
content: JUNE 2022 © MarketsandMarkets™
The production can be optimized even further by creating process digital twins of all the manufacturing
equipment involved in performing that specific process. By using the data from process digital twins,
businesses can prevent costly downtime to equipment and even predict when preventative maintenance
will be necessary. This constant stream of accurate information enables manufacturing operations that are
faster, more efficient, and reliable.

sections.heading: SYSTEM DIGITAL TWIN
content: A system digital twin is a collection of products and processes that together perform as a system- or
network-wide function, such as an oil and gas refinery/plant, production line in a factory, assembly line,
traffic network, wind farm, or hospital. A system twin provides visibility into a set of interdependent
equipment. A system twin is simply the next step up from a product twin. They are most frequently
implemented in the same software product as product or component twins, but they are just a perspective
of the entire system. For instance, in an energy production plant, a system twin (depending on its
definition) might reflect the past and current condition of a power plant, the entire power plant, or even a
partition of a power grid, and anticipate future state. System twins provide insight into asset interactions
and may recommend performance improvements.
A system digital twin generates a large amount of data regarding their (different assets within a system)
utilization and effectiveness. This data is analyzed and processed for the betterment of the systems and
improving the system performance by reducing the faults and taking preventive measures. It also provides
actionable insight for informed decision-making. By leveraging system digital twins, companies can:

sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
content: The digital twin market, on the basis of enterprise size, has been categorized into small & medium-sized
enterprises (SMEs) and large enterprises. This chapter categorizes the end users (demand side) of digital
twin products/solutions on the basis of their enterprise size. It is to be noted that this chapter does not
indicate or represent the digital twin providers (supply side) on the basis of their enterprise size.
These organizations are categorized according to the number of employees and global standards. The
study of the market according to enterprise size is important since it provides a clear picture of the
adoption scenario of digital twin technology, solutions, and services across enterprises of various sizes.
According to the current trends, all types of enterprises, either large or SMEs, are witnessing technological
disruptions in the digital age that are impacting engineering, manufacturing, operations, and service
legislation. Intelligent and linked goods are expected to deliver continuous and real-time engineering data,
while deeper insights into the generated data will enable cognitive contextualization.
As digital twins become more capable, they are being applied to a growing number of uses in SMEs and
large enterprises, from designing and testing products and processes to monitoring day-to-day operations
and conducting maintenance. Digital twin has emerged as a critical technology for use in the early stages
of product development. It can enable enterprises to forecast system performance in the future and be
used to create a digital thread with data from connected smart devices. Digital twins reduce the amount of
time engineering teams spend iterating a product, lowering the overall product life cycle expenses. On the
other hand, the complimentary/related technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning
(ML), internet of things (IoT), industrial IoT, extended reality (augmented reality, virtual reality, and mixed
reality), and blockchain-as-a-service (BaaS) enable faster adoption of digital twin solutions. Furthermore,
over decentralized networks, BaaS for IoT can provide better solutions with benefits such as scalability,
security, interoperability, cost-effectiveness, and reduced operational complexity. As a result, blockchain
may be a better candidate for IoT digital twin networks than centralized networking systems.
Digital twin solutions implemented across the supply chain collect data in real time over the network in the
supply chain. The processes/products/equipment across supply chain can be linked using an IoT network,
which ensures the authenticity of the information/products/services and builds trust, transparency, and
security throughout the organization as well as among the customers and clients.

content: A digital twin of a physical object or an asset combines all available information and analytical models of
the object throughout its life cycle. The technology is increasingly being used to describe a means of
connecting information about the physical product and its behavior in the real world with 3D digital
representation, which is commonly employed during engineering and in other areas of the business. For
instance, Dassault Systems (France) introduced the virtual twin concept that enables design and
engineering teams to visualize and analyze the products or systems virtually and also provides insights
similar to physical behaviors, including stress and vibration as well as behaviors associated with the
software and control systems.
It provides end users with insights into their factory performance by monitoring the key performance
indicators in real time across all systems in the facility and providing rapid access to vital business data. At
the same time, it provides traceability, improves transparency, and tracks issues during operations.

content: For monitoring the health and performance of any asset/equipment/machinery, digital twin creates a
simulated replica throughout the life cycle of that product. These applications are subsequently used with
machine learning algorithms to optimize operational downtime, trigger pre-emptive maintenance, and
mitigate costly failures. In a manufacturing organization, product manufacturing, production, asset life
cycle management, and health monitoring play a vital role. With the increasing innovation in manufacturing
organizations, rising demand for production efficiency and competitive pressure, there would be a rise in
demand for digital twins for optimizing processes.
The performance monitoring applications of digital twin include the assessment of production process and
the final product itself. The digital twin platform receives data from the product and the manufacturing
facilities on a regular basis, resulting in new insights. Performance monitoring improves the dependability
and availability of a system. As a successful technique for improving system performance, digital twins
facilitate monitoring, modeling, and control of an asset, process, or network. For example, GE (US) provides
SmartSignal and Asset Performance Management (APM) solutions that generate digital twins from
operational/fleet data of components (pumps or compressors), essential assets (turbines), or asset
systems (an entire power station). The solutions assure product quality by facilitating real-time monitoring
of asset and process performance, allowing customers to improvise and react to modification while
minimizing supply chain impact.

content: Predictive maintenance offered by digital twin increases content productivity, thereby enabling improved
ongoing operations, maintenance, and service. This virtual copy of a product enables better
communication and collaboration among organizations or manufacturers for product management,
manufacturing, supply chain management, and service offering. For example, a digital twin of a wind
turbine with intelligent data processing capability enables predictive maintenance of its behavior and
condition. Also, the virtual models combine mathematical models to describe the physics of the turbine
operation, with sensor data collected and processed from real assets during real-world operations. This
would benefit the wind farm operators to predict structural failure and plan maintenance activities with
greater accuracy, in advance. As a result, operators can reduce the maintenance costs and operational
downtime during the life cycle of wind turbines.

Businesses can save money and gain a competitive advantage by taking this approach. Digital twin

In the infrastructure industry, digital twin plays a vital role in optimization of the entire operations of
modern and smart buildings. Cities and huge university campuses benefit from real-time digital twins
because they provide a robust platform for modelling, understanding, and analyzing interconnections
between buildings, electrical systems, and other public infrastructure. Digital twins collect data from a
variety of sources and intelligently combine it with other data sets, capturing context and relationships. For
instance, in September 2021, the Brooklyn Navy Yard in the US hired Cityzenith (US), a digital twin
software developer, to create digital twins for a group of buildings, systems, and infrastructure at the Navy
Yard. The digital twins will be used to automate real-time energy monitoring, onsite renewable energy
generation, and carbon offset purchases at the Brooklyn Navy Yard.

utilized to develop a Virtual Campus Energy Model to help the Dundalk Institute of Technology (Ireland) to
achieve its goal of becoming a net-zero energy campus, offering analysis and knowledge of the dynamics in
their distributed energy network. The solution focuses on delivering both environmental analysis of

engines, machines, and other parts. In the aerospace industry, digital twins help minimize the cost of
production, optimize processing, and reduce production time. Digital twins combined with augmented and
virtual reality help the companies in better involvement of customers at the earlier stage in the design
process, thereby minimizing the need for expensive late-stage changes in the design and saving time.
Governments of various countries worldwide are initiating new projects to transform infrastructure and
security systems for developing aircraft, satellites, and other space technologies. The use of digital twins in
the aerospace industry facilitates collaborative and synchronized program management to be applied
across the product life cycle and value chain. The implementation of digital twin technology in the
aerospace industry was initiated by National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) (US) to monitor
and operate complex systems in remote and critically hazardous conditions. The technology has the ability
to record real-time telemetry data and process it quickly to represent it into model-based simulations,
which is valuable in remote, demanding, or dangerous industrial processes. Businesses in the aerospace
industry can benefit from digital twins in a variety of ways, including prolonging the life of parts and
machines and leveraging data to better the next iteration. Aerospace businesses can employ digital twins
in research and development to improve the engineering of new parts by simulating their performance
under a wide range of situations. A digital twin can predict how an engine would perform in adverse
conditions; or what will the airline's performance be like after 300+ flights. This information may now be
gathered and used to enhance parts, forecast when maintenance is required, and increase the life of
